source_read: PDF, Addiction 113: 1339–1344 (all 6 pages, text layer); Results and Table 1 (pp. 1340–1341) checked on pages rendered at 150 dpi; supporting Table S1 not in the PDF and not seen; yearly corrections recomputed from Table 1

claims.overstatement: The '21% to 36% a year' is not printed in the paper. The paper prints 21–35% for any opioid (p. 1340; the abstract gives 20–35% across both categories). Recomputed from Table 1, the yearly excess runs from 20.9% (2015) to 35.7% (2008), so 36% is an editors' rounding: label it as an editors' calculation or use the printed 21–35%. The heading 'Certificates that name no drug' is slightly wider than the paper: Ruhm measures coded drug involvement (only T50.9, which he describes as unspecified drugs, medicaments and biologicals), not the certificate's words. The claim sentence itself ('no specific drug identified') matches.
claims.note: 568,699, 23.1%, 26.0% (2008), 17.2% (2015), 33,091 and 39,999 all match the rendered pages. 39,999/33,091 = 1.209, the printed 21%. The claim correctly presents the corrected figures as model estimates, untested against toxicology or case records. The paper's only comparison is with a 'naive' division method built on the same assumption, and it states that no confidence intervals were computed. The correction raises drug-specific counts only for deaths coded with no specific drug, so it can only add involvement, and it leaves total drug deaths unchanged. The Table 1 text layer drops minus signs (heroin/synthetic 2000 row: −69, −47, −2.6%, −1.4% on the rendered page); scripts that read the text layer should allow for this.

anchors.extracted: 1999–2015: 42,170,818 deaths of US residents, including 568,699 fatal drug poisonings. Specific drug involvement was not specified in 23.1%: highest 26.0% in 2008, lowest 17.2% in 2015, falling steadily since 2008 with no clear pattern before.

anchors.locator: Methods, 2nd paragraph (top of p. 1340; paragraph number corrected after step 2 on the rendered page)
anchors.extracted: Drug poisoning means underlying cause X40–X44, X60–X64, X85 or Y10–Y14, i.e. all intents. Opioids are T40.0–T40.4 and T40.6; heroin/synthetic opioids are T40.1 and T40.4. In one-sixth to one-quarter of overdose deaths, depending on the year, only T50.9 (unspecified drugs, medicaments and biologicals) was coded.

anchors.locator: Methods, 3rd and 4th paragraphs; Table 1 note (p. 1341) (paragraph numbers corrected after step 2 on the rendered page)
anchors.extracted: Reported counts give no drug category to deaths coded only T50.9. The correction fits year-specific probit models to deaths with at least one drug category coded, using demographics and their interactions, day of week, place of death and 2010 county characteristics. It then predicts opioid involvement for the T50.9-only deaths, i.e. it assumes they resemble similar deaths with a named drug.

anchors.locator: Table 1 (Any opioid, 2015 row); Discussion, 2nd paragraph; Results, 2nd paragraph (p. 1340)
anchors.extracted: Any opioid, 2015: 33,091 reported against 39,999 corrected (+21%). Heroin/synthetic opioids: 19,884 against 23,857 (+20%). Corrected counts were 21–35% higher than reported for all opioids and 20–35% for heroin/synthetic opioids. Recomputed from Table 1: 20.9% (2015) to 35.7% (2008) for any opioid.
The correction raises the counts and rates for specific drug categories without changing the total number of drug deaths.

A simpler 'naive' method divides reported rates by the share of deaths with at least one drug specified. For 2011 (74.7% specified) it gives 9.79 and 3.01 per 100,000, against 9.83 and 2.99 from the full model. This compares two methods resting on the same assumption; it is not an external check.

The author lists six limitations: (1) only deaths with no drug specified are adjusted, so multi-drug deaths still understate specific drugs; (2) certificate drug mentions can be wrong, e.g. heroin attributed to morphine or codeine; (3) codes lack specificity (T40.6 unspecified narcotics; T40.4 groups fentanyl with other synthetic opioids); (4) drug deaths may be attributed to non-drug causes or the reverse; (5) data are assumed missing at random given the covariates; (6) no confidence intervals were computed.

Budget limits on toxicology testing and autopsies, which give the most accurate information, mean corrections will remain necessary for trends that otherwise partly reflect changing reporting accuracy. The data used contain no toxicology field.

key_findings.correction: Confirmed. Recomputed from Table 1: 20.88% (2015) to 35.67% (2008) for any opioid; 19.98% to 34.56% for heroin/synthetic.
Confirmed. 23,857/6,140 = +288.6% against the printed 287%; the other 2007–2015 figures reproduce within rounding.

reporting_issues.note: Confirmed: 26,567/19,582 = 1.357. I would rather the claim label 36% as an editors' calculation than cite '21–36%' as the paper's range.

risk_of_bias.note: I agree with JBI-prevalence, overall high, for the corrected counts the paper is cited for. The census figures (568,699 deaths; 23.1% with no specific drug) carry low risk as descriptions of what was coded. Confirmed on the Table 1 note: no state or investigation-system covariate is in the model.

interpretation_gap.note: I would rate this 'substantial' rather than 'minor', on the card's own evidence. The abstract presents a single model prediction as 'the actual number' (approximately 39,999) and calls imputation likely more accurate, and the Discussion says it stays considerably more accurate even if missing-at-random fails. None of this was tested against toxicology or case records, and no uncertainty is given. The abstract also misdescribes the largest differences. The body is transparent, so this is borderline; the difference is logged for the senior author.
